rule: Provider operators must raise an Airflow exception type (`AirflowException`, `AirflowFailException`, `AirflowTaskTimeout`) when a deferred trigger reports an error or timeout; never raise a bare `RuntimeError`
trigger: An `execute_complete()` (or other trigger-event handler) body contains `raise RuntimeError(event["message"])` or another non-Airflow builtin exception on the failure/timeout branch
rationale: Airflow classifies task failures by exception type; a bare `RuntimeError` breaks consistent failure semantics for users and conflicts with the deferrable-operator patterns used everywhere else in the same operator

evidence.excerpt: raising `RuntimeError` makes it harder to classify failures consistently
Raising a bare `RuntimeError` here is inconsistent with the rest of this operator
raise one consistent Airflow exception type for timeouts/errors

rule: Imports of a provider's optional extra dependencies must be wrapped in `try/except ImportError` and re-raised with a message naming the extra to install (e.g. `apache-airflow-providers-akeyless[cloud_id]`)
trigger: A function body imports a third-party package that is declared as an optional extra rather than a required provider dependency, without a surrounding `try/except ImportError`
rationale: Users who select an auth/feature path without installing the extra otherwise get a bare `ImportError` with no indication of which extra to install

evidence.excerpt: Catch `ImportError` and raise a clearer exception that explains how to install the dependency

rule: Provider howto `.rst` pages must describe the typical use case for each operator, not merely restate or link the underlying boto3/vendor API call
trigger: A new `providers/*/docs/operators/*.rst` page consists only of `literalinclude` example blocks plus a Reference link to the vendor API documentation
rationale: Provider documentation is user-facing; describing only the wrapped API call leaves users unable to tell when they should reach for the operator

evidence.excerpt: worth adding a sentence or two describing the typical use case for each operator

rule: Do not add per-task INFO logging to an executor's scheduler-loop methods; submission acknowledgements belong at debug level and exceptions already collected into `failure_reasons` must not be logged again individually
trigger: A new `self.log.info(...)` call is added inside `attempt_task_runs()` or another per-task loop in an executor, especially one reporting success on API acceptance or echoing an exception that is also appended to `failure_reasons`
rationale: The executor loop runs for every task on every scheduler iteration, so per-task INFO lines are log spam; a successful control-plane submission is also not task success, since the task can still fail in ECS or in the container

evidence.excerpt: This doesn't mean it was successful per se, just that the control plane accepted
we should fix that instead of logging each one to reduce spam

rule: Do not alias the `airflow.executors.workloads` import (`import workloads as wl`) to dodge a name collision; rename the local parameter instead
trigger: An executor method such as `_process_workloads` declares a parameter named `workloads` and the body then does `from airflow.executors import workloads as <alias>`
rationale: The aliased import exists only because the parameter shadows the module name, adding confusion for no benefit; the parameter is the thing that should be renamed

evidence.excerpt: Rename the parameter and you don't need the added confusion of the `as`

rule: A change that silently alters which driver, backend or default an existing provider user gets must be recorded in that provider's `docs/changelog.rst` in the same PR
trigger: A hook rewrites a connection URI drivername, swaps a client library, or changes a default without a corresponding entry added to `providers/<name>/docs/changelog.rst`
rationale: Users with both libraries installed are moved from one driver to another with no signal; the changelog is the only place they would learn their runtime changed

evidence.excerpt: a Redshift user with both drivers installed silently moves from psycopg2 to psycopg3

rule: Name generator/paginating hook methods with an `iter_` prefix (`iter_file_metadata`), not `yield_`
trigger: A new public hook method that yields items is named `yield_*` or otherwise not prefixed `iter_`
rationale: Airflow's established prefix for lazy iteration helpers is `iter_`; `yield_` describes the implementation mechanism rather than the returned iterator

evidence.excerpt: probably `iter_file_metadata` would be better

rule: Use `state` rather than `status` for the lifecycle-value parameter and comparisons in a module whose surrounding code already speaks in terms of state
trigger: A new helper such as `_handle_state(...)` takes a parameter named `status` while the neighbouring code, constants and comparisons in the same module use `state`
rationale: Mixing the two terms in one module makes the state comparisons read as if they operate on a different concept than the surrounding code

evidence.excerpt: We're using state everywhere else so the comparisons look a bit strange.

rule: Operator-link persistence called from `execute_complete()` must be guarded on the required context keys being present (e.g. `context.get("task_instance")`) rather than assuming a full task-instance context
trigger: `execute_complete()` unconditionally calls a `_persist_links`/`*Link.persist(context)` helper that dereferences `context["task_instance"]`
rationale: This repo's unit tests invoke `execute_complete` with an empty dict, and the persist path additionally makes AWS API calls, so an unguarded call raises instead of resuming the task

evidence.excerpt: In this repo's unit tests `execute_complete` is invoked with an empty dict

rule: Operator-link persistence helpers must return early when `self.do_xcom_push` is False, before making any provider API call needed to build the link
trigger: A `_persist_*_link()` helper calls a hook/describe API to assemble link data and then calls `SomeLink.persist(...)` without first checking `do_xcom_push`
rationale: `Link.persist()` is a no-op when xcom push is disabled, so the preceding describe call is a wasted (and billed) provider API request

evidence.excerpt: Consider returning early in `_persist_cloudwatch_link()` when `not self.do_xcom_push` to avoid unnecessary AWS API usage

rule: Do not downgrade a caught `AirflowException` from a log/metadata lookup to INFO with a transient-sounding message; keep it at warning unless the transient case is distinguished from the error case
trigger: An `except AirflowException` handler around a call like `get_job_all_awslogs_info()` is changed from `self.log.warning` to `self.log.info` with wording such as "not yet available"
rationale: The same exception is also raised for non-transient conditions such as an unsupported job type, so the reassuring INFO message hides real configuration problems

evidence.excerpt: this message/level is misleading and can hide real configuration issues

rule: Service state categories (terminal, modifiable, stopped sets) must live on the hook and be composed from the hook's existing state enum, not redefined as tuples/frozensets on the operator
trigger: A new operator or trigger class declares module- or class-level state groupings such as `TERMINAL_STATES = frozenset({...})` with literal state strings while the hook already exposes a state enum
rationale: Operator and trigger both need the same categories; duplicating them on the operator invites code drift, and a new enum alongside the existing one fragments the state vocabulary

evidence.excerpt: better to just reuse the existing enum class instead of creating a new enum class

rule: A public operator `__init__` parameter must not be reduced to a stored-but-unread attribute; either keep the behaviour it selects or remove the parameter as an explicit breaking change
trigger: A refactor assigns `self.<param> = <param>` for a documented operator parameter (e.g. `wait_policy`) while `execute()` stops consulting it and reads a derived flag instead
rationale: Operator constructor parameters are public API; leaving one assigned but inert silently drops documented behaviour for users who still pass it

evidence.excerpt: The `wait_policy` is still being stored but never used in the execute method.

rule: `execute_complete()` must branch explicitly on each trigger event status; do not treat everything that is not `success` as a single failure/cancel path
trigger: `execute_complete` checks `if validated_event["status"] == "success": return ...` and then falls through to cancellation or failure handling for all remaining statuses
rationale: A status added to the trigger later is silently swallowed into the cancel path; explicit status branches keep the operator's resume semantics honest as the trigger evolves

evidence.excerpt: In the future another status might get swallowed into this path

rule: Wrap boto3 calls in `except botocore.exceptions.ClientError`/`BotoCoreError` rather than `except Exception`, so programming errors propagate instead of silently taking the fallback path
trigger: A `try` block around a boto client call (`self.hook.conn.<api>(...)`) is followed by `except Exception` with a `log.warning` and a fall-through to the default behaviour
rationale: A broad handler also swallows `KeyError`/`AttributeError` from the response-parsing code, so the operator quietly reverts to the behaviour the change was meant to prevent (e.g. duplicate job runs)

evidence.excerpt: Catch boto exceptions more narrowly (e.g., `botocore.exceptions.ClientError` / `BotoCoreError`) and let unexpected exceptions propagate

rule: AWS operators must build `template_fields` with the `aws_template_fields(...)` helper instead of unpacking `*AwsBaseOperator.template_fields` into a manual tuple
trigger: A class deriving from `AwsBaseOperator` declares `template_fields: tuple[str, ...] = (*AwsBaseOperator.template_fields, "foo", "bar")`
rationale: `aws_template_fields()` is the pattern used throughout the Amazon provider; hand-unpacking the base tuple is the older form that was simply never cleaned up in this module

evidence.excerpt: there is a cleaner way that is used throughout AMPP

rule: A method named as a deferral resume callback (`method_name=` on `self.defer(...)`) must take `context` as its first positional parameter, with `event` and any extra state as keyword arguments
trigger: A method passed as `method_name="..."` to `self.defer()` declares a domain parameter (e.g. `import_task_id`) before `context`
rationale: Airflow resumes a deferred task by calling `method(context, **next_kwargs)` with `event` injected into `next_kwargs`, so a leading domain parameter raises `TypeError: multiple values for argument` at resume time

evidence.excerpt: Airflow calls the next method as `method(context, **next_kwargs)` (with `event` injected into `next_kwargs`)

rule: Expose new hook functionality as explicit optional parameters on the hook method rather than smuggling it through `**kwargs` from the operator
trigger: An operator builds a dict of extra arguments and passes it as `**extra_args` into a hook method (e.g. `copy_object`) whose signature does not name those parameters
rationale: Adding optional parameters is non-breaking and makes the contract part of the public API; `**kwargs` forwarding leaves the behaviour dependent on an undocumented pass-through that tests alone must protect

evidence.excerpt: Adding optional parameters would be non-breaking here and would make the contract more explicit

rule: Hooks must normalise vendor API responses into the snake_case keys their operators consume; operators must not index a raw boto response key the hook never produces
trigger: An operator reads `response["some_snake_case_id"]` from a hook call whose implementation returns the raw boto response (e.g. `{"notebookRunId": ...}`) as the tests demonstrate
rationale: The mismatch is invisible until runtime, where it raises `KeyError`; the hook is the layer that owns translating the vendor response shape

evidence.excerpt: This will raise a `KeyError` at runtime unless the hook normalizes the response (recommended)
